reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Usually autosomal dominant, with the common form (type 1) linked to contraction of the D4Z4 repeat array on chromosome 4q35, leading to aberrant expression of the DUX4 gene
Weakness characteristically begins in facial muscles, often with difficulty closing the eyes, whistling, or smiling, before descending to the shoulder girdle
Scapular winging with difficulty raising the arms above the head is a hallmark, and the deltoid is often relatively spared
Weakness is frequently asymmetrical, which is an unusual and helpful diagnostic feature among the dystrophies
Foot drop from anterior tibial weakness and abdominal muscle weakness (with a positive Beevor sign) are common
Extramuscular features can include high-frequency hearing loss and retinal vascular changes (Coats-like retinopathy), especially in severe early-onset disease
Diagnosis is confirmed by specialised genetic testing of the 4q35 locus rather than routine muscle biopsy
Management is supportive, with physiotherapy, scapular fixation surgery in selected cases, and treatment of foot drop and pain
reference.pathophysiology: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy arises from failure to silence the DUX4 gene within the D4Z4 macrosatellite repeat region on chromosome 4q35. In the common type, contraction of the repeat array reduces the normal epigenetic repression of this region, and in the rarer type variants in chromatin-modifying genes have a similar effect. Inappropriate expression of DUX4, a transcription factor normally silent in mature muscle, is toxic to muscle fibres and triggers a cascade of gene activation leading to muscle degeneration. The distinctive facial, scapular, and often asymmetrical pattern of weakness reflects the selective vulnerability of these muscle groups.
additionalInvestigations: Specialised molecular genetic testing of the 4q35 D4Z4 locus
Serum creatine kinase, which is normal or only mildly elevated
Muscle MRI to document the pattern and asymmetry of involvement
Audiometry and retinal examination in early-onset or severe disease
Baseline respiratory function testing in advanced disease
redFlags: Symptomatic retinal vascular disease threatening vision in severe early-onset cases
Respiratory compromise in advanced or severe disease
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Early-onset infantile disease with systemic complications
reference.prognosis: Progression is usually slow, most patients have a normal lifespan, and a minority eventually require wheelchair support. Severe early-onset disease is associated with a greater burden of weakness and extramuscular complications such as hearing and retinal involvement.
pitfalls: Overlooking subtle facial weakness and attributing scapular winging to a local shoulder problem
Expecting a markedly raised creatine kinase, which is often only mildly elevated
Not recognising asymmetry as a characteristic feature
Relying on muscle biopsy rather than the specific genetic test
Missing hearing and retinal complications in early-onset disease
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists, so care is supportive and rehabilitation-focused
Physiotherapy and low-impact aerobic exercise to maintain strength and prevent contractures, with occupational therapy for function
Ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop and mobility aids to reduce falls
Scapular fixation surgery (scapulothoracic arthrodesis) for selected patients with disabling scapular winging
Analgesia and management of musculoskeletal pain and complications
Surveillance including respiratory function testing in advanced disease, and audiometry with dilated retinal examination in early-onset or severe cases
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular team involvement, with genetic counselling and family assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance
